content.title: Why isn't Nasa using SpaceX for Artemis?
content.text: SpaceX isn’t missing from Artemis. It’s just waiting for the landing phase. SpaceX has become NASA’s most visible commercial partner, flying astronauts to the International Space Station and landing rockets with routine precision. So why isn’t SpaceX launching astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II? At first glance, it does seem strange. The answer lies in how NASA structured the Artemis program years before SpaceX’s Starship was flight-ready. Artemis II, the mission that will send four astronauts on a lunar flyby, is built around NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and the Orion crew capsule. SLS was authorized by Congress in 2011, long before Starship existed, with a mandate to use legacy Space Shuttle and Constellation-era hardware. The rocket is powerful, but it’s also the product of traditional aerospace contracting and long development timelines. SpaceX is part of Artemis, just not this mission. In 2021, NASA selected SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) to land astronauts on the Moon during Artemis III. However, that version of Starship requires orbital refueling, multiple tanker launches, and successful large-scale testing that is still underway. NASA has acknowledged that Starship’s development pace and testing milestones directly influence the Artemis III schedule. Artemis II, by contrast, does not require a lunar lander. It’s a crewed test of SLS and Orion in deep space, essentially validating NASA’s own system before attempting a landing. So it’s not that SpaceX isn’t going to the Moon. It’s that Artemis is a hybrid program. NASA’s rocket for the first crewed return, and SpaceX’s vehicle for the landing phase, once it’s fully ready.
